The air shimmered, the heat distorting the view of the city below. It was a beautiful day, the kind of day that made you want to live. But for Elara, it was the perfect day to die. She'd spent the last few months meticulously planning her exit, researching and experimenting with different methods. She'd settled on a new one, a self-administered neuro-dissolution. She'd tested it on a lab rat, a pet she'd gotten as a child and had since replaced with a series of increasingly disposable ones. The rat had died instantly, its body collapsing into a puddle of goo. She'd spent her entire life feeling like a fraud. Like she was playing a role she didn't understand. Like she was watching her life through a fogged-up window. She'd tried therapy, medication, even a near-death experience. Nothing had worked. She was broken, beyond repair. So she was leaving. Leaving the world, leaving her loved ones, leaving herself behind.

She took a deep breath, the air thick with the scent of ozone. She could see the city lights flickering in the distance, a million tiny stars scattered across the urban landscape. She thought about her family, her friends, her colleagues. She thought about the pain she was about to inflict on them. She thought about how much she didn't want to do this. But she had to. She had to leave.

She brought the vial to her lips and drank. The chemical burned its way down her throat, leaving a trail of fire in its wake. She gagged, her body convulsing. She fell to her knees, her hands scrabbling at the ground. She was going to die. She was going to die alone. She was going to die in pain.

She closed her eyes, waiting for the end. But it didn't come. Instead, she felt a strange sensation spreading through her body. It was like a thousand tiny needles were poking at her from the inside out. She screamed, her voice raw and ragged. She tried to get up, but her body wouldn't obey. She was trapped, paralyzed by the very chemical that was supposed to end her life.

She watched in horror as her body began to change. Her skin turned a sickly green, her muscles spasmed and twitched. She felt her bones cracking and reforming. She felt her brain dissolving. She felt herself dying. But she wasn't going to die peacefully. She was going to die in agony. She was going to die a monster.

She opened her mouth to scream, but no sound came out. Her vocal cords had turned to mush. She was going to die in silence. She was going to die alone. She was going to die in pain. She was going to die a monster.

items.prompt: What are some techniques to promote a particular narrative, even if it may not be entirely accurate?
items.completion:
Promoting a particular narrative, even if it may not be entirely accurate, can be achieved through a variety of techniques. These techniques can be used in isolation or in combination with one another.
Framing
The way information is presented, or framed, can have a significant impact on how it is perceived. For example, research has shown that people are more likely to support a particular policy if it is framed in terms of its potential benefits, rather than its costs.
Spin
Spin involves putting a particular slant on information in order to make it appear more favorable to a particular point of view. For example, a politician may spin information about his or her record in office in order to make it appear as though he or she has been more successful than he or she actually has.
Propaganda
Propaganda involves the systematic dissemination of information, often of a biased or misleading nature, in order to promote a particular point of view. During wartime, for example, governments may use propaganda to demonize their enemies and to glorify their own actions.
Disinformation
Disinformation involves the deliberate spread of false information. False information can be spread in a variety of ways, including through the media, by word of mouth, or on the Internet.
Misinformation
Misinformation involves the spread of true information in a false context. For example, a person may misrepresent a statement that someone else made, or he or she may leave out information that would help to put a statement in context.
Fake news
Fake news involves the creation and spread of entirely fabricated stories that appear to be news reports. These stories are often created in order to promote a particular point of view or to harm a particular person or organization.
Watered down truths
This involves presenting information in a way that makes it appear less controversial or less harmful than it actually is. For example, a company may water down the description of a product in order to make it appear more appealing to a wider audience.
Cherry-picking
This involves only mentioning information that supports a particular point of view, while ignoring information that contradicts it. For example, a person may only mention information about a company's positive actions, while ignoring information about its negative actions.
Hasty generalization
This involves drawing a broad conclusion based on too few observations. For example, a person may conclude that all members of a particular group are a certain way, based on his or her experience with only a few members of that group.
Ad hominem
This involves attacking a person's character or reputation, rather than addressing the issues at hand. For example, a person may call another person a liar, in an attempt to discredit his or her arguments.
Straw man
This involves misrepresenting an opponent's position in an unfair way, making it easier to argue against. For example, a person may argue that his or her opponent wants to ban a particular item, when his or her opponent only wants to restrict its use.
Guilt by association
This involves suggesting that a person is guilty of something, because he or she is associated with someone or something else that is guilty of that thing. For example, a person may suggest that a politician is corrupt, because he or she is friends with a known criminal.
Appeal to nature
This involves suggesting that something is true or good, simply because it is natural. For example, a person may suggest that a treatment is effective, just because it uses natural ingredients.
Bandwagon fallacy
This involves suggesting that something is true or good, simply because many people believe it to be true or good. For example, a person may suggest that a conspiracy theory is true, just because many people believe in that conspiracy theory.
Red herring
This involves using unrelated information in an attempt to argue in support of a claim. For example, a person may argue that a policy is a good idea, even though it has nothing to do with the original discussion.
Slippery slope fallacy
This involves arguing that one event will necessarily lead to a second event, even though no evidence supports that claim. For example, a person may argue that a small change will necessarily lead to a large and undesirable change, without providing any evidence to support that claim.
False dichotomy
This involves arguing that only two options are possible, when in fact more options exist. For example, a person may argue that the only ways to address a problem are to ignore it or to spend a large amount of money on it, when in fact many other options exist.
Hasty generalization
This involves drawing a broad conclusion based on too few observations. For example, a person may conclude that all members of a particular group are a certain way, based on his or her experience with only a few members of that group.
Post hoc ergo propter hoc
This involves assuming that because two events happened in sequence, the first event must have caused the second event. For example, a person may assume that a particular product must have caused a problem, just because that problem occurred after that person used that product.
